title: Taylor v. Caldwell
lead: Concert promoters arrange four events at a particular music hall, then lose the venue to an accidental fire. Their preparation expenses lead the court to ask whether the owners promised performance despite the hall’s destruction.

actors.name: Taylor and Lewis
actors.role: Promoters responsible for concert artists and publicity.

actors.name: Caldwell and Bishop
actors.role: Owners promising use of the Surrey Gardens and Music Hall and related entertainment services.

proceedings: A trial verdict favored the promoters, with leave reserved to enter a defense verdict on the second and third issues.
The Queen’s Bench made the rule absolute to enter a verdict for the owners.
limits: This is a source-brief transformation, not a fresh audit or current frustration-law review. The report identifies the argument panel but no numerical judgment vote or separate opinion. Its civil-law examples concern historical slavery and are authorities invoked by the court, not facts of this transaction. The court was Queen’s Bench despite the assigned caption’s label.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The parties arrange a coordinated entertainment venture
sections.cue: Why was this particular hall central?
paragraphs: On May 27, 1861, Caldwell and Bishop agreed to give Taylor and Lewis use of the Surrey Gardens and Music Hall for concerts and day-and-night fêtes on June 17, July 15, August 5, and August 19. The promoters would pay £100 at the end of each day and keep entrance receipts.

The owners were to provide an organized military and quadrille band, other amusements, fireworks, and illuminations; the promoters supplied concert artists and advertising. Terms governed advertising access, when dancing could begin, and the latest fireworks hour. The bargain therefore concerned coordinated performances at the particular hall, not simply access to outdoor land.

sections.title: An accidental fire destroys the venue before the first event
sections.cue: What loss did the promoters seek to shift?
paragraphs: On June 11, the hall burned. The accidental destruction was extensive enough to prevent the contemplated concerts, and neither side was at fault. Their agreement contained no express provision allocating this event.

Taylor and Lewis sued for money spent advertising and preparing performances, alleging failure to provide the promised facilities. At trial before Justice Blackburn, they obtained a verdict subject to reserved leave to enter a defendants’ verdict on the second and third issues. The owners obtained a rule seeking that result. Counsel argued in January 1863 before Chief Justice Cockburn and Justices Wightman, Crompton, and Blackburn.

sections.title: The court reads the promise in light of its necessary subject
sections.cue: Why did positive language not make the promise unconditional?
paragraphs: The promoters argued that, despite the words “let” and “rent,” this was no demise transferring possession. They also relied on Paradine v. Jane, a precedent for enforcing absolute contractual obligations despite accidental impediments. The owners argued that it was a demise and that “God’s will permitting” qualified the whole transaction.

Delivering judgment, Blackburn agreed that the owners retained possession and granted use on specified days, so there was no demise, but said nothing ultimately turned on that characterization. Nor did the holding depend on the proposed construction of “God’s will permitting.” The agreement as a whole showed that the intended performances could not take place without this hall.

An absolute promise to do a lawful act ordinarily required performance or damages even when an unforeseen accident made performance burdensome or impossible. Yet promises could carry express or implied conditions. Where continued existence of a particular person or thing was fundamental, and the promisor did not expressly or impliedly warrant its existence, innocent destruction before breach could excuse performance.

The court inferred the condition from the nature of the transaction: persons considering such a contingency ordinarily would provide for it. It did not find that these parties actually discussed or anticipated the fire; the disaster had not been in their contemplation.

sections.title: Analogies explain both the condition and its limits
sections.cue: What kinds of prior obligations remained distinct?
paragraphs: The court drew guidance from Roman law concerning specific subjects and from Pothier’s treatment of destruction without the debtor’s act, neglect, or prior default, while expressly denying that civil law itself governed an English court. The Roman examples used enslaved persons as subjects of historical obligations.

English personal-service examples included an author dying before completing a work, loss of necessary capacity, and death of an apprentice whose father promised the service. The essential person could therefore be someone other than the promisor, and an unqualified promise without an express death clause did not foreclose an implied condition.

The court also considered specific goods destroyed after ownership passed and duties to return particular chattels. Rugg v. Minett illustrated that payment consequences could depend on whether title had passed; the analysis did not undo every prior risk allocation or promise refunds universally. Williams v. Lloyd illustrated excuse for innocent loss of a particular thing where the promisor neither assumed the risk nor caused the loss. Coggs v. Bernard and earlier bailment authorities helped show that the principle belonged to English law rather than being only an imported rule.
These analogies supported implying continued existence from the performance’s nature even when the promise used positive terms.

sections.title: The owners receive a defense verdict
sections.cue: How did the discharge operate on both sides?
paragraphs: Because this particular Music Hall was essential, its faultless destruction before the first performance date excused both sides. Taylor and Lewis no longer had to take the gardens and pay the price. Caldwell and Bishop no longer had to supply the hall, gardens, and related services. The promoters could not recover their preparation losses as damages for nonperformance.

On May 6, 1863, the court made the rule absolute to enter a verdict for the defendants, replacing the conditional plaintiffs’ verdict. Blackburn delivered the judgment; the report supplies no separate concurrence or dissent and no numerical judgment vote.
